files.label: Database Overview
files.summary: The full GFXR-to-SQLite schema and the relationships between every table.
description: A comprehensive view of every table in the GFXR database, their columns, and the foreign-key relationships that tie them together. Use this diagram as the canonical reference when writing queries, designing ETL steps, or onboarding to the data model.

Column types are not indicated here except when a column references an enum table. In those cases the enum type is listed after the column name in (parentheses). Enum tables are not explicitly shown in the diagram as displaying them would clutter an already busy view. Most foreign key references are shown via a line and arrow connection, except where adding one would make the diagram unreadable. In most cases, those references that are not shown are called out with a note.
Each section of the diagram will be covered in detail using the navigation buttons to the right.

files.label: Core GFXR Data
files.summary: The core data tables that anchor everything else in the schema.
description: Core GFXR Data tables include frame and low-level API event tracking. This is essentially the raw data of the GFXR file. In GFXReconstruct terminology, apiEvent is equivalent to a block index. As such, this will include both Vulkan commands and GFXReconstruct meta events.

API event tracking includes the function name, all of the command arguments that were passed to the original function call, and its return value. Note that the value members here are all TEXT columns. They have a type field that contains a TEXT column describing the type of the value field. This is intended only for recursive display of function call arguments and not for typed comparison. It is difficult to work with these tables directly within queries, as they require recursive joins and lack typed columns. The rest of the database design is intended to structure this information for more useful and efficient queries.
Try an apiEventArguments query

Each apiEvent has an apiEventType that indicates whether the apiEvent is a Vulkan command or a GFXReconstruct meta command. GFXReconstruct uses meta commands to record pre-capture trim state restoration commands (such as FillMemoryCommand) and to track frame markers (FrameEndMarker). These can be useful, if not required, to be supported by the implementing applications.
Try a META_COMMAND query

Database versioning is handled through the standard SQLite PRAGMA user_version.
The encoding formula is: (GFXR_DB_VERSION_MAJOR * 10000) + (GFXR_DB_VERSION_MINOR * 100) + GFXR_DB_VERSION_PATCH.
Try a user_version query
GFXReconstruct metaData, annotations, and displayMessages are all specific to .gfxr files and do not represent Vulkan constructs.

files.label: Debug Utils/Markers
files.summary: The data tables used to track debug markers and debug utils extensions.
description: Debug markers and labels are both stored as debugLabels in the database, as these serve the same purpose to graphics tooling. Note that they have a lifecycle via beginApiEvent and endApiEvent. This provides grouping information to allow for nested commands within a debug label group. Insertion labels will have matching begin/end apiEvent values as their "group" is the label itself.

Debug labels have two types: queue labels and command buffer labels. Both are stored in the same debugLabels table. Queue labels will have a NULL for the commandBufferRecordingId and render pass/subpass columns, as they do not live within a command buffer.
Try a debug queue labels query
For convenience, the gfxr-sqlite database generates a queueDebugLabels lookup table after database construction that can be used to help identify these.

Binary data for debugTags, debugReportCallbacks, and debugMessengers is not inserted into the gfxr-sqlite database. Instead, it should be retrieved from the .gfxr file directly if needed by the implementing application.

debugReportCallbacks do not contain the function pointer address of the callback, as it would not be relevant in any future replay and the function itself cannot be decoded from .gfxr files at database creation time.

files.label: Command Tree Relevant Data
files.summary: Tables that participate in command-tree traversal and analysis.
description: The slice of the schema relevant to command-tree work: the tables that describe commands, draws, dispatches, state groups, and the parent/child links between them.
Command tree objects follow the pattern of Vulkan queue-based frame submissions.

At the top level we have the frames table, which tracks all frames in the capture. A frame boundary is recorded via the FrameEndMarker meta command, triggered by the presence of a vkQueuePresentKHR command or a vkQueueSubmit command that contains a VkFrameBoundaryKHR struct in its pNext chain. On Android, FrameEndMarker could also be triggered by a vkFrameBoundaryANDROID. Frames are scoped using the beginApiEventId and endApiEventId columns. Any queue commands whose apiEvents fall between these two markers are typically related to the frame unless parallel frame submission is occurring.

Next are queue and device-level commands. These include the queueSubmits themselves, which are organized into batches of command buffers. It typically also includes an acquireNextImages and queuePresents entry unless this is an offscreen application and does not utilize swapchains and the vkQueuePresentKHR command. For convenience, each of these commands contains a frameId column to help map these commands to the frame they were executed within. The trackedDeviceCommands are a list of device-level commands that do not have tables of their own as they do not have additional information that has been worth tracking. These may eventually be broken into their own tables if there is a need to track them individually.
Try a queue commands by frame query

Below a queue submission (within their batch/submission buffer groups) are the commandBufferRecordings. These will always be recordings of primary command buffers because only primary command buffers can be submitted directly to a queue. CommandBufferRecordings are scoped by their beginApiEventId, endApiEventId and resetApiEventId columns, with the reset being either an explicit vkResetCommandBuffer command or an implicit reset through a new vkBeginCommandBuffer command. Recordings are different from the Vulkan object they are associated with. There is an N to 1 relationship between recordings and the associated object as the object is reused multiple times throughout the capture.

Another thing to keep in mind is that recordings happen PRIOR to submission. This means that the beginApiEventId and endApiEventId of the recording will be LESS THAN the queueSubmit.apiEventId of the queue submission. Also, a commandBufferRecording might be submitted multiple times (as is the case in our sample data).

To help handle multi-threaded command buffer recording scenarios, commands that are associated with a specific command buffer recording are also inserted into the commandBufferCommands table for easy lookup, as simple apiEvent range-based filtering is insufficient.
Try a queue submission command buffer recordings by frame query

Within the commandBufferCommands entries are the commands that are recorded to the command buffer. These include secondaryCommandBufferExecutionRecordings which track command buffer recordings submitted through vkCmdExecuteCommands, renderPassRecordings for traditional render passes, and dynamicRenderPassRecordings for the more modern dynamic rendering. Each of these can contain additional child commands, typically pipeline/buffer/descriptor set bindings and draw commands. Secondary command buffer executions can be recursive to some depth. State tracking tables are not shown on this diagram and are covered in the Draw/Dispatch state tracking section.

commandBufferRecordings can also have trackedCmdCommands that are similar to trackedDeviceCommands except that they track vkCmd* type commands that do not have explicit tables for them. transferCommands are similar in that they group all transfer commands such as vkCmdCopyBuffer and vkCmdBlitImage. These are typically handled together by the implementing application, so separate tables for each were deemed unnecessary.

For the primary commands of interest (vkCmdDraw*, vkCmdDispatch, vkCmdTraceRaysKHR) there are individual tables to track the recording events of each of these.
Try a draw recording by frame query

files.label: Vulkan Enum Types
files.summary: Tables that enumerate and decode Vulkan enum values used throughout the schema.
description: The Vulkan enum structs are populated through code generation. The tables are not individually listed in any of the diagrams as they would clutter the diagrams unnecessarily. Each table has value, valueName, and aliasName columns. VkBool32 is explicitly called out here as it is not populated by code generation.

The aliasName columns are essentially the valueName columns but they strip the prefix and postfix portions of the valueName and convert from snake case to spaces.
Try a VkImageCreateFlagBits query

files.label: Pipeline State
files.summary: Tables that describe pipeline objects and their static configuration.
description:
The tables that record graphics and compute pipeline static state configuration: shader stages, fixed-function state, and parameters set at pipeline-creation time.
Try a pipeline state query

Note that this covers only static state configurations; dynamic state tracking is handled by a separate set of tables, as dynamic state requires additional tracking mechanisms. See Draw/Dispatch State Tracking.

files.label: Lifecycle Tracking
files.summary: Tables that track the creation, use, and destruction of resources.
description: The slice of the schema concerned with object lifetimes: when handles are created, how they are used over the course of a capture, and when they are destroyed. These mirror the Vulkan object types and provide typed columns for the majority of the create info struct members.

Note that lifecycle tracking is handled using paired apiEventIds (sometimes triplets in the case of objects that can be reset and reused). Typically these are a createApiEventId and a destroyApiEventId. Note that these events take place at the device level and will be sequentially ordered with queue submissions (also shown in this diagram). This is different from the commandBufferCommands entries that track recording time and should be treated as children of a commandBufferRecordings entry (possibly nested under render pass/subpass as well). Applications may want to display the lifecycle of objects relative to a 'filter event', which is typically a frames.apiEventId or queueSubmits.apiEventId.
Try a filtered image lifecycle query
Every table is created in the database, even if a capture does not contain a specific class of objects. The table will simply be empty if there are no objects of that type.

files.label: Relevant Command Tracking
files.summary: Tables that track the commands relevant to a given analysis.
description: As mentioned in the Command Tree Relevant Data section, there are some commands that are not the primary commands of interest (Draws/Dispatches/TraceRays) but that applications would still want to display in the command tree. There are two categories of these:

The first are transferCommands which include commands like vkCmdCopyBuffer and vkCmdBlitImage. These commands all perform data transfers and have join tables that contain the information regarding the buffer/image/buffer-image transfer. These are typically handled by the same node type in the implementing command tree so there isn't a compelling reason to track them independently. They are always cmd commands and as such are included in the commandBufferCommands entries.

The second are trackedDeviceCommands and trackedCmdCommands. These are other commands that applications may want to include in their command trees, such as memory and synchronization operations. trackedDeviceCommands are device-level commands that live outside a queue submission. trackedCmdCommands are cmd commands and as such are included in the commandBufferCommands entries.

files.label: Acceleration Structure Build Tracking
files.summary: Tables that track ray-tracing acceleration structure builds.
description: The slice of the schema dedicated to acceleration structure build/copy operations: their inputs and the resulting structures used by ray-tracing workloads.
Currently, these only track KHR acceleration structure builds/copies. NVIDIA builds/copies are not tracked in these tables.

files.label: Draw/Dispatch State Tracking
files.summary: Tables that track the state bound at each draw and dispatch.
description: The state tracking tables capture the state in effect at the moment each draw or dispatch executes: bound pipelines, descriptor sets, vertex/index buffers, and other dynamic state.

State changes for each command buffer are tracked at construction time. When any given draw or dispatch recording is encountered, if the associated state has changed, a new stateGroups.id is assigned. Note that this table is virtual, meaning it does not exist in the database. It is simply an incrementing number that the gfxr consumer uses to group stateGroupEntries. The additional state/binding tables track the actual dynamic state or pipeline/descriptor set bindings that were modified by the command.

commandBufferRecordings and secondaryCommandBufferExecutions also track stateGroupIds for the purpose of supporting command buffer state inheritance. This is typically only applicable when the Vk_NV_command_buffer_inheritance extension is supported and enabled.
